newsitem.title: UK: Hardy Oil sees growth, acquisitions.
newsitem.headline: Hardy Oil sees growth, acquisitions.

text.p: Hardy Oil and Gas Plc is set for a period of growth after refocusing itself and could see acquisitions later this year, its chief executive said on Tuesday.
"The refocusing we began two years ago is now complete," John Walmsley said in a statement accompanying the group's nine month results.

To help finance the oil and gas exploration group's biggest ever drilling programme and the expected go-ahead of some of its big developments, Hardy agreed a 200 million pound ($317 million) credit facility with a group of banks.

"We've (now) got the money to develop the oil projects, to fund the exploration programme and to grow the business, and that obviously will at some point involve us making acquisitions or (purchasing) assets," Walmsley told Reuters in a telephone interview.
At 1155 GMT, Hardy shares were up 6-1/2 pence at 322 pence, down from a high of 333 reached in January but up from a low of 261 seen at the beginning of this month.
With the company in the growth stage and with a good team in place, Walmsley said he would expect "during the course of the year to put something on the books".

Walmsley was speaking after the company announced a net profit of 5.7 million pounds in the nine months to December 31, 1996, against a loss of 6.6 million pounds in the year to March 31. Previously the company said it was changing its year end from March 31 to December 31.
Walmsley said the nine month figures represented an "excellent period", in which Hardy not only improved financially but also added new reserves and successfully appraised some recent discoveries.
Reserves at the end of 1996 amounted to 88 million barrels of oil equivalent (mboe) against 54 mboe at the end of March 1996.
"Shareholders have every reason to look forward with confidence to the coming year," Walmsley said.
The group plans total capital expenditure in 1997 of 80 million pounds, of which around 20 million will be for exploration and appraisal.
"This represents a significant increase over the level of expenditure in previous years," the company said in a statement accompanying the results.
Hardy plans 17 exploration and appraisal wells this year and is actively pursuing opportunities for growth in its core areas of the UK Continental Shelf, Australia and Pakistan, as well as India.
Developments in these areas are seen trebling Hardy Oil's production in the next six years.
'It's a pretty reasonable set of results,' said Colin Smith, analyst with ING Baring Securities Ltd, who added this was basically on the back of higher oil prices.

However, Baring's Smith warned: "The numbers at the moment don't really mean that much for Hardy because an awful lot of the value of the group is in assets which are going to come on in the year 2000 and beyond, that's where the bulk of this movement up to tripling current production levels actually comes from."

Asked if he saw the company as the potential target for a takeover bid, Walmsley said: "Hardy at the moment is into its stride and that would not be in the slightest bit welcome or necessary as far as the company's progress is concerned."
Walmsley takes the view that a firm oil price in 1997 would be a bonus but is not something to depend on.

The company has a "terrifically strong balance sheet, we've now got the credit facility, our developments are pretty low cost developments per unit, so they're the strong core of the business -- if the price is weak, fine, we'll get on."
